questions.stem: Consider this: A lawyer researching a disputed point finds a conflict between a statute and a prior decision. The legislature later amended the statute. Which statement best states the governing legal rule?

Any published rule has the same force as a statute because publication makes it law in this situation.
A valid statute outranks a regulation or local custom that conflicts with it, because subordinate sources derive their force from the legislature in the present case.
A regulation overrides a statute whenever the agency has more expertise about the subject in this situation.

questions.explanation: Legal sources are ordered. A legislature may delegate rulemaking, but a subordinate rule that departs from the enabling statute fails, and customary practice cannot displace an enacted command. Here the decisive point is the hierarchy among enacted law and subordinate rules, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask which source derives its authority from which. Keep the inquiry on the hierarchy among enacted law and subordinate rules.
